title: Java Mastery Question Bank
description: 240 Java questions with answers and explanations, organized by topic.

questions.question: What is the output? int x = 5; System.out.println(x++ + ++x);
questions.explanation: x++ evaluates to 5, then x becomes 6. ++x increments it to 7 and evaluates to 7. The sum is 12.

questions.question: What is the output? int x = 10; System.out.println(x++ + x++);
questions.explanation: Operands are evaluated left to right: the first yields 10, the second yields 11.

questions.question: What is the output? int x = 0; boolean result = false && (++x > 0); System.out.println(x);
options: false
Compilation error
questions.explanation: && short-circuits when its left operand is false, so the right operand is not evaluated.

questions.question: What is the output? int x = 0; boolean result = true || (++x > 0); System.out.println(x);
options: true
Compilation error
questions.explanation: || short-circuits when its left operand is true.

questions.question: What is the difference between && and & for booleans?
options: & short-circuits; && evaluates both operands.
&& short-circuits; & evaluates both operands.
They are identical for booleans; only precedence differs.
&& works only on ints; & works only on booleans.
questions.explanation: Both can combine booleans, but only && skips the right operand when the left operand determines the result.

questions.question: What is the difference between || and | for booleans?
options: | short-circuits; || evaluates both operands.
They are identical for booleans; only precedence differs.
|| short-circuits; | evaluates both operands.
|| works only on ints; | works only on booleans.
questions.explanation: || skips the right operand when the left operand is true; | evaluates both.

questions.question: Does Java have the general comma operator found in C/C++?
options: No; Java only allows commas as separators, such as in for-loop headers and argument lists.
Yes, anywhere an expression is allowed.
Yes, but only inside method calls.
Yes, but only in switch statements.
questions.explanation: Java uses commas as separators in syntax such as argument lists and declarations, but it has no general C/C++-style comma operator.

questions.question: What is printed by System.out.println(10 / 3); and System.out.println(10 / 3.0);?
options: 3, then 3.0
3, then 3
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates the fractional part; floating-point division preserves an approximate fraction.

questions.question: What is printed by System.out.println(-7 / 2); and System.out.println(-7 % 2);?
options: -4, then 1
-3, then -1
-3, then 1
-4, then -1
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero; the remainder has the sign of the dividend.

questions.question: What is the output? System.out.println(1 + 2 + "Java" + 3 + 4);
options: 12Java34
3Java7
3Java34
1Java34
questions.explanation: Evaluation proceeds left to right. After string concatenation begins, subsequent + operations concatenate strings.

questions.question: What is the output? System.out.println("Java" + 1 + 2); System.out.println(1 + 2 + "Java");
options: Java12, then 3Java
Java3, then 3Java
Java12, then 12Java
Java3, then 12Java
questions.explanation: The first expression begins with a string; the second performs integer addition before concatenation.

questions.question: What is the output? System.out.println(10 > 5 ? 1 : 2.5);
options: Compilation error
questions.explanation: The conditional expression's numeric type is double, so the integer branch is promoted.

questions.question: What is the output? int x = 5; x += 2.5; System.out.println(x);
options: Compilation error
questions.explanation: Compound assignment includes an implicit conversion back to the left-hand type.

questions.question: Does this compile? int x = 5; x = x + 2.5;
options: Yes; x becomes 7 after implicit narrowing.
Yes; x becomes 7.5 because x is promoted to double.
Yes, but it throws an exception at runtime.
No; the double result needs an explicit cast to be assigned to an int.
questions.explanation: The expression is double and cannot be implicitly narrowed to int in an ordinary assignment.

questions.question: What is the result of System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);?
options: true
Compilation error
false
ArithmeticException at runtime
questions.explanation: These decimal fractions are generally not represented exactly in binary floating point.

questions.question: What happens when int x = 10; System.out.println(x / 0); executes?
options: Infinity
NaN
Compilation error
ArithmeticException at runtime
questions.explanation: Integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException.

questions.question: What is printed by 1.0 / 0.0 and 0.0 / 0.0?
options: ArithmeticException for both
NaN, then Infinity
Infinity, then NaN
Infinity, then Infinity
questions.explanation: Floating-point division follows IEEE 754 behavior; positive finite divided by positive zero yields positive infinity, and zero divided by zero yields NaN.

questions.question: What are the results of 5 & 3, 5 | 3, and 5 ^ 3?
questions.explanation: These are bitwise AND, OR, and XOR.

questions.question: What are the results of 1 << 3 and 16 >> 2?
options: 8 and 8
3 and 2
8 and 4
4 and 8
questions.explanation: The operators shift bits left and arithmetic-right, respectively.

questions.question: What is the difference between >> and >>> in Java?
options: >>> preserves the sign bit; >> always fills with zeros.
>> works on int only; >>> works on long only.
>> is arithmetic right shift; >>> is logical right shift with zero-fill.
>> shifts left; >>> shifts right.
questions.explanation: For signed integers, >> preserves the sign bit while >>> fills leftmost positions with zeroes.

questions.question: How many primitive types does Java have, and what are they?
options: Eight: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, String.
Nine: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean, String.
Eight: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean.
Seven: byte, short, int, long, float, double, boolean.
questions.explanation: These are Java's eight primitive types.

questions.question: What are default values for instance fields, and do local variables get defaults?
options: Both fields and local variables receive type-specific defaults.
Fields receive type-specific defaults; local variables must be definitely assigned before use.
Neither fields nor local variables get defaults; both must be assigned.
Local variables get defaults; fields must be assigned before use.
questions.explanation: Numeric primitives default to zero, char to '\u0000', boolean to false, and references to null.

questions.question: Does Java char always represent one complete Unicode character?
options: Yes. char is a 32-bit Unicode code point.
Yes. char is an 8-bit ASCII value.
No. char is a 32-bit UTF-32 code unit.
No. char is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit.
questions.explanation: Some Unicode code points require a surrogate pair of two char values.

questions.question: What is printed by char c = 'A'; System.out.println(c + 1); System.out.println((char)(c + 1));?
options: B, then B
66, then B
A1, then B
66, then 66
questions.explanation: Arithmetic promotes char to int; the cast converts the result back to char.

questions.question: What is printed by byte b = 127; b++; System.out.println(b);?
options: ArithmeticException
questions.explanation: Increment narrows the result back to the signed 8-bit byte type, wrapping around.

questions.question: Does byte b = 10; b = b + 1; compile?
options: Yes; the literal 1 is a byte so the sum stays a byte.
No; b + 1 is an int and needs an explicit cast to be assigned back to byte.
Yes, but it throws an exception at runtime.
Yes; the compiler narrows automatically because the value fits in a byte.
questions.explanation: The addition is performed as int and needs an explicit narrowing conversion.

questions.question: Does byte b = 10; b += 1; compile?
options: No; b + 1 is an int and needs an explicit cast.
Yes; compound assignment includes an implicit cast.
No; byte does not support += at all.
Yes, but only if b is declared final.
questions.explanation: Compound assignment includes implicit narrowing conversion.

questions.question: What are autoboxing and unboxing?
options: Automatic conversion between a primitive and its corresponding wrapper type.
Converting a primitive to a String and back automatically.
Implicit casting between int and long during arithmetic.
Automatically moving objects between the stack and the heap.
questions.explanation: For example, int can be boxed to Integer and Integer unboxed to int.

questions.question: What happens when Integer n = null; int x = n; executes?
options: x becomes 0
ArithmeticException
Compilation error
NullPointerException
questions.explanation: Unboxing a null wrapper reference throws NullPointerException.

questions.question: What is printed by Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; System.out.println(a == b);?
options: false
Compilation error
NullPointerException
true
questions.explanation: Java guarantees caching for boxed constant integer values from -128 through 127.

questions.question: For separately boxed Integer values of 1000, is a == b guaranteed true or false?
options: Neither result is guaranteed; == compares references.
Always true, because == on Integer compares values.
Always false, because boxed values are never cached.
It always fails to compile for boxed comparison.
questions.explanation: The language does not require identical wrapper objects for values outside the mandatory cache range. Use equals() for value comparison.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and equals() for objects?
options: == compares contents; equals() compares references.
== compares references; equals() follows the class's equality implementation.
They are identical for all objects.
== works only on primitives; equals() works only on strings.
questions.explanation: Object's default equals() is identity-based, but many classes override it for value equality.

questions.question: What is the difference between widening and narrowing conversions?
options: Widening needs a cast and may lose data; narrowing is implicit and safe.
Widening converts to a broader type; narrowing may lose information and usually requires a cast.
Widening converts between objects; narrowing converts between primitives.
Widening applies only to int; narrowing applies only to double.
questions.explanation: For example, int to long is widening, while double to int is narrowing.

questions.question: What is printed by (int) 3.9 and (int) -3.9?
options: 3 and -4
3 and -3
4 and -4
4 and -3
questions.explanation: Floating-point to integer casts truncate toward zero.

questions.question: What is printed by String a = "hello"; String b = "hello"; followed by a == b and a.equals(b)?
options: false, then true
true, then false
true, then true
false, then false
questions.explanation: Identical string literals are interned, and their contents are equal.

questions.question: What is printed when two separately constructed new String("hello") objects are compared with == and equals()?
options: true, then true
true, then false
false, then false
false, then true
questions.explanation: They are distinct objects but contain equal text.

questions.question: What is printed by String a = "Ja" + "va"; String b = "Java"; System.out.println(a == b);?
options: false
true
Compilation error
It depends on the JVM
questions.explanation: Compile-time constant string concatenation is evaluated at compile time and uses the interned string.

questions.question: For String a = "Java"; String b = a + "!"; String c = "Java!";, what is b == c?
options: true, because both strings have the same characters
false in this example
true, because the compiler interns b
Compilation error
questions.explanation: Concatenation involving a variable creates a string not guaranteed to be identical to the literal; equals() compares contents.

questions.question: How do you obtain the canonical interned string instance?
options: Call canonical().
Call String.valueOf().
Call toString().
Call intern().
questions.explanation: intern() returns the canonical pooled representation.

questions.question: What does it mean that String is immutable?
options: Its variable cannot be reassigned once declared.
It cannot be compared with ==.
Its contents cannot change after construction.
Its length is fixed but its characters can be replaced.
questions.explanation: Immutability enables safe sharing, predictable hashing, pooling, and thread-safe use of string state.

questions.question: Compare String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer.
options: String is mutable; StringBuilder and StringBuffer are immutable.
StringBuilder is synchronized, StringBuffer is unsynchronized, and String is immutable.
All three are immutable and differ only in memory usage.
String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and unsynchronized; StringBuffer is mutable with synchronized methods.
questions.explanation: StringBuilder is generally preferred for local string construction; synchronization does not make arbitrary multi-operation logic automatically safe.

questions.question: What is printed by String s = "hello"; s.toUpperCase(); System.out.println(s);?
options: HELLO
null
hello
Compilation error
questions.explanation: toUpperCase() returns a new string rather than modifying the original.

questions.question: What does String.length() count compared with codePointCount()?
options: length() counts UTF-16 code units; codePointCount() counts Unicode code points in a range.
length() counts code points; codePointCount() counts UTF-16 code units.
length() counts bytes; codePointCount() counts characters.
They always return the same value.
questions.explanation: A supplementary Unicode code point occupies two UTF-16 code units.

questions.question: If int[] a = {1,2,3}; int[] b = a; b[0] = 9;, what is a[0]?
options: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
questions.explanation: Both variables refer to the same array object.

questions.question: What is the initial value of a[0] for int[] a = new int[3]?
options: null
Undefined until assigned
questions.explanation: Array elements are initialized to their type's default value.

questions.question: What happens when int[] a = null; System.out.println(a.length); executes?
options: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
NullPointerException
Compilation error
questions.explanation: Dereferencing a null array reference throws NullPointerException.

questions.question: Does Java support jagged multidimensional arrays?
options: No; all rows must have the same length.
No; only rectangular arrays are supported.
Yes, but only for arrays of objects, not primitives.
Yes; rows of a multidimensional array can have different lengths.
questions.explanation: A multidimensional array is an array of arrays, whose rows can have different lengths.

questions.question: How can you print an int array's elements in readable form?
options: Use array.toString().
Use System.out.println(array) directly.
Use array.print().
Use Arrays.toString(array).
questions.explanation: Printing the array reference directly does not print its elements.

questions.question: Can Dog[] be assigned to Animal[] when Dog extends Animal?
options: No; array types are invariant in Java.
Yes; Java arrays are covariant.
Yes; but only with an explicit cast.
No; Dog[] and Animal[] are unrelated types.
questions.explanation: The runtime array type still enforces its actual component type.

questions.question: What happens with Object[] a = new String[1]; a[0] = 42;?
options: ClassCastException at runtime
ArrayStoreException at runtime
Compilation error
It stores the string '42'
questions.explanation: The actual array can store only String values, even though the reference type is Object[].

questions.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
options: A class defines a type; an object is a runtime instance.
A class is a runtime instance; an object is a type definition.
They are the same thing.
A class holds only static members; an object holds instance members.
questions.explanation: Classes define fields and methods; objects hold instance state.

questions.question: Can Java constructors be overloaded?
options: No; constructors share the class name so they cannot be overloaded.
Yes, but only if they have different return types.
Yes, but only one may be public.
Yes, by using different parameter lists.
questions.explanation: Constructors are not distinguished by return type.

questions.question: Does a constructor have a return type?
options: Yes, it returns the new object.
Yes, always void.
Yes, it returns the class type.
No; it has only the class name and parameters.
questions.explanation: A declaration with the class name and a return type is a method, not a constructor.

questions.question: When does the compiler provide a default no-argument constructor?
options: Always, even if other constructors are declared.
When the class declares no fields.
When the class declares no constructors.
When the class is declared public.
questions.explanation: Declaring any constructor suppresses automatic generation of the default constructor.

questions.question: Can a constructor be private, and why?
options: No; constructors must be public or package-private.
Yes; it can control object creation, support factories or singleton patterns, or prevent instantiation.
Yes, but then the class can never be instantiated by any code.
No; private constructors are allowed only in enums.
questions.explanation: Private constructors are accessible only where Java's access rules permit.

questions.question: Can a constructor be static, final, or abstract?
options: No; none of these modifiers are allowed on constructors.
Yes, any of them is allowed.
Only final is allowed.
Only static is allowed, for factories.
questions.explanation: Those modifiers do not apply to constructors.

questions.question: Can a top-level class be private?
options: Yes; private restricts it to its own file.
Yes; private makes it package-private.
No; a nested class can be private.
No; and nested classes cannot be private either.
questions.explanation: Top-level classes can use public or package-private access.

questions.question: Can a top-level class be static?
options: No; only nested classes can be static.
Yes; it makes the class a singleton.
Yes; it allows access without instantiation.
Only if it has no constructors.
questions.explanation: A nested class can be static; a top-level class cannot.

questions.question: How does a static nested class differ from a non-static inner class?
options: A static nested class holds an enclosing instance; an inner class does not.
A static nested class cannot have instance members; an inner class can.
They are identical except for syntax.
An inner class is associated with an enclosing instance; a static nested class is not.
questions.explanation: A static nested class does not require an enclosing object to be instantiated.

questions.question: If static int x = 10 is declared in A, then a.x = 20, what does b.x print for another A instance b?
options: Compilation error
questions.explanation: A static field belongs to the class and is shared by instances.

questions.question: What is the difference between static and instance methods?
options: Static methods have this; instance methods do not.
Static methods can be overridden; instance methods cannot.
Instance methods belong to the class; static methods belong to each object.
Static methods belong to the class; instance methods execute in an object context and have this.
questions.explanation: Static methods cannot directly access instance members without an object reference.

questions.question: Can a static method directly access an instance variable?
options: Yes, because instance variables are shared by all objects.
Yes, but only if the variable is public.
No; it needs an object reference to access instance variables.
Yes, by using this.
questions.explanation: It needs an object reference to access instance state.

questions.question: What does this refer to?
options: The current class.
The superclass object.
The most recently created object.
The current object.
questions.explanation: It can distinguish fields from parameters and invoke another constructor using this(...).

questions.question: What is super used for?
options: Accessing superclass implementations or invoking a superclass constructor.
Referring to the current object's fields.
Declaring a class abstract.
Calling a static method of a subclass.
questions.explanation: super(...) invokes a superclass constructor.

questions.question: Can a constructor contain both this(...) and super(...) as explicit constructor invocations?
options: Yes; this(...) must come first and super(...) second.
Yes, but only in a private constructor.
No; neither is allowed explicitly in Java.
No; only one explicit constructor invocation is allowed.
questions.explanation: Traditional syntax requires it to be first; Java 25 flexible constructor bodies permit certain statements before it.

questions.question: What is constructor chaining?
options: A constructor calling an overridden method.
One constructor invokes another constructor in the same class or a superclass.
Creating a chain of objects with linked references.
Declaring multiple constructors with different parameters.
questions.explanation: It supports reuse of initialization logic and proper superclass initialization.

questions.question: In what order do instance field initializers and initializer blocks run?
options: In reverse textual order, before superclass initialization.
In textual order, after superclass initialization and before the remaining constructor body.
Initializer blocks first, then field initializers, then superclass initialization.
Before superclass initialization, in textual order.
questions.explanation: The order applies to the instance initialization sequence for that class.

questions.question: At a high level, what happens during object creation?
options: Memory is allocated, fields receive defaults, superclass and instance initialization run, then constructor bodies execute.
Fields get defaults, constructor bodies run, then memory is allocated.
Superclass constructors run after the subclass constructor body.
Memory is allocated and constructors run, but fields are left uninitialized.
questions.explanation: Static initialization is part of class initialization rather than each object's creation.

questions.question: What are Java's four access levels?
options: public, protected, default, and final.
public, private, static, and abstract.
public, private, package, and global.
public, protected, package-private, and private.
questions.explanation: Package-private is represented by omitting an access modifier.

questions.question: What does package-private mean?
options: Accessible only within the same class.
Accessible within the same package, subject to Java's other rules.
Accessible from any package.
Accessible only in subclasses.
questions.explanation: No access modifier gives package-level access.

questions.question: What does protected mean?
options: Accessible within the package and in qualifying subclass contexts outside it.
Accessible only in the same class.
Accessible only within the same package.
Accessible only from subclasses in the same package.
questions.explanation: Cross-package subclass access has specific restrictions.

questions.question: Can a private method be overridden?
options: Yes, using the @Override annotation.
Yes, but only in a nested class.
Yes, if the subclass is in the same package.
No; private methods are not inherited, so they cannot be overridden.
questions.explanation: Private methods are not inherited as overridable methods; a same-signature subclass method is separate.

questions.question: Can a class have private fields and public methods?
options: No; fields and methods must share the same access level.
No; public methods cannot access private fields.
Yes; fields are typically private with public accessor methods.
Only in abstract classes.
questions.explanation: This is a common encapsulation pattern.

questions.question: Can code inside a class access a private field on another instance of that same class?
options: No; private fields are accessible only through the same instance.
No; only through getters.
Yes; private is class-scoped, not instance-scoped.
Only if the class is final.
questions.explanation: Private access is based on class access rights, not only the current object.

questions.question: Does final on an object reference make the object immutable?
options: Yes; final makes the object immutable.
No; it prevents reassignment of the reference, not mutation of the referenced object.
Yes; final prevents the object's fields from changing.
No; final prevents the object from being garbage collected.
questions.explanation: A final StringBuilder reference can still call append().

questions.question: Distinguish final, finally, and finalize().
options: final is a modifier; finally is an exception-handling block; finalize() is a deprecated legacy cleanup hook.
final is an exception block; finally is a modifier; finalize() is a garbage collection method.
All three are modifiers that prevent inheritance, overriding, and reassignment.
final is a modifier; finally is a cleanup hook; finalize() is an exception-handling block.
questions.explanation: finalize() is deprecated for removal and should not be used for resource management.

questions.question: What is method overloading?
options: Methods with the same name and same parameters in a subclass.
Methods share a name but have different parameter lists.
Methods with different names but identical parameter lists.
A subclass replaces a superclass method with the same signature.
questions.explanation: Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.

questions.question: What is method overriding?
options: Methods in the same class share a name but have different parameters.
A subclass declares a static method with the same name as the superclass.
A class declares a method with the same name but a different return type.
A subclass provides a compatible implementation of an inherited instance method.
questions.explanation: Normal overridable instance calls dispatch according to the runtime object type.

questions.question: If A has show() printing A, B extends A overrides show() to print B, and A obj = new B(); obj.show() is called, what prints?
options: A
AB
Compilation error
B
questions.explanation: Overridden instance methods use dynamic dispatch based on the runtime object.

questions.question: If A overloads show(Object) and show(String), and Object x = "hello"; new A().show(x) is called, which overload is selected?
options: show(String)
Compilation error (ambiguous)
show(Object)
The overload is chosen at runtime from the object's type
questions.explanation: Overload resolution uses the compile-time type of the argument.

questions.question: If A and B each declare static show(), and A obj = new B(); obj.show() is called, which body runs?
options: B's static show()
Compilation error
It depends on the runtime type of obj
A's static show()
questions.explanation: Static methods are hidden, not overridden; selection uses the compile-time type.

questions.question: Can a static method and an instance method override one another with the same signature?
options: Yes; the static method replaces the instance method.
No; a static method cannot override an instance method, nor vice versa.
Yes, but only if both are in the same package.
Yes, if the static method is declared final.
questions.explanation: The declarations conflict and cause a compile-time error.

questions.question: Can an overriding method reduce visibility?
options: No; an overriding method cannot have weaker access than the overridden one.
Yes; overriding methods may reduce visibility.
Yes, but only from public to protected.
Yes, but only for static methods.
questions.explanation: The override cannot be less accessible than the overridden method.

questions.question: Can an overriding method declare broader checked exceptions?
options: Yes; overriding methods may declare any checked exception.
No; it cannot declare new or broader checked exceptions than the overridden method.
Yes, but only if declared with throws Exception.
Yes, but only for abstract methods.
questions.explanation: It may declare narrower checked exceptions or none; unchecked exceptions are not restricted in the same way.

questions.question: Can an overriding method change its return type?
options: No; the return type must always match exactly.
It may use a covariant reference return type; primitive return types must match.
Yes; both primitive and reference return types may change freely.
Yes; but only primitive return types may be widened.
questions.explanation: The replacement reference type must be a subtype of the original return type.

questions.question: If A has int x=10, B extends A with int x=20, and A obj = new B(); what does obj.x print?
options: Compilation error
questions.explanation: Fields are hidden, not dynamically overridden; field access uses the compile-time reference type.

questions.question: A superclass constructor calls an overridable method, and the subclass override prints an int field initialized to 10. What can it print during superclass construction?
options: null
A compilation error
questions.explanation: The override can run before subclass field initializers, so the field still has its default value.

questions.question: What is polymorphism?
options: Defining multiple classes with the same name in different packages.
Using a common supertype for different concrete objects while overridden methods behave according to runtime type.
Using one class name for several unrelated variables.
Overloading methods so the compiler picks one by argument types.
questions.explanation: Dynamic dispatch enables subtype-specific behavior through a common API.

questions.question: Does Java support multiple inheritance of classes?
options: Yes; a class may extend multiple classes.
Yes, but only with abstract classes.
No; a class can implement multiple interfaces.
No; and a class cannot implement multiple interfaces either.
questions.explanation: Java classes have one direct superclass.

questions.question: Are constructors inherited?
options: Yes; subclasses inherit all accessible constructors.
No; constructors are not inherited by subclasses.
Only public constructors are inherited.
Only no-argument constructors are inherited.
questions.explanation: A subclass constructor must invoke an appropriate superclass constructor, explicitly or implicitly.

questions.question: What if a superclass has only parameterized constructors and a subclass declares no constructor?
options: It compiles; the subclass gets a default constructor that skips super().
It compiles; the superclass constructors are inherited by the subclass.
A runtime exception is thrown when the subclass is instantiated.
Compilation fails if the generated no-argument subclass constructor cannot call an accessible super().
questions.explanation: The compiler-generated default constructor attempts a no-argument superclass invocation.

questions.question: What is the difference between instanceof and a cast?
options: instanceof throws ClassCastException when incompatible; a cast returns false.
They are identical operations written differently.
instanceof converts the object; a cast only tests compatibility.
instanceof tests type compatibility; an incompatible non-null reference cast throws ClassCastException.
questions.explanation: instanceof returns false for null.

questions.question: What does null instanceof String evaluate to?
options: true
NullPointerException
false
Compilation error
questions.explanation: Null is not an instance of any reference type.

questions.question: Can a final class be extended?
options: Yes, using the extends keyword.
Yes, but only within the same package.
No; a final class cannot be subclassed.
Yes, but only by an abstract class.
questions.explanation: final prevents subclassing.

questions.question: Can a final instance method be overridden?
options: Yes; final only prevents reassignment.
Yes, but only in a subclass in the same package.
Yes, if the override is also declared final.
No; a final method cannot be overridden.
questions.explanation: final prevents overriding.

questions.question: Can an abstract class contain no abstract methods?
options: Yes; an abstract class may declare zero abstract methods.
No; abstract classes must have at least one abstract method.
No; it would then be an interface.
Only if it is declared final.
questions.explanation: It may be abstract simply to prevent direct instantiation.

questions.question: Can an abstract class have a constructor?
options: No; abstract classes cannot have constructors.
Only if all methods are abstract.
Yes; it runs when a subclass is constructed.
Only a private constructor is allowed.
questions.explanation: Its constructor runs during construction of a concrete subclass object.

questions.question: Can an abstract class be instantiated directly?
options: Yes, using the new keyword.
Yes, but only if it has no abstract methods.
No; it can only be instantiated through a concrete subclass.
Yes, if it has a public constructor.
questions.explanation: Concrete subclasses can be instantiated and referenced through the abstract type.

questions.question: Can an abstract method be private, static, or final?
options: Yes; abstract methods may be private, static, or final.
No; those modifiers conflict with the need to be overridden.
Only private is allowed.
Only static is allowed.
questions.explanation: Those modifiers conflict with the requirement that an implementation be supplied through inheritance.

questions.question: Can interfaces contain implemented methods?
options: No; interfaces can only have abstract methods.
Yes: default, static, and (since Java 9) private methods.
Only default methods are allowed.
Yes, but only static and abstract methods.
questions.explanation: Interfaces may also declare abstract instance methods.

questions.question: What modifiers are implicit for interface fields?
options: private static final
protected static
public static final
public final
questions.explanation: Interface fields are constants and must be initialized at declaration.

questions.question: Are all interface methods necessarily public?
options: Yes; all interface methods are public.
No; since Java 9, interface methods may be private.
No; they are package-private by default.
Yes; except for static methods, which are private.
questions.explanation: Java 9+ permits private interface methods; ordinary abstract and default methods are public.

questions.question: What must a class do if it inherits conflicting default methods from two interfaces?
options: Nothing; the compiler picks the first interface listed.
Nothing; the compiler picks the one declared in the alphabetically earlier interface.
Resolve the conflict, usually by overriding the method.
It must mark the method final.
questions.explanation: A concrete class must disambiguate conflicting interface defaults.

questions.question: When a superclass implementation conflicts with an interface default method, which takes precedence?
options: The interface default method.
Whichever was declared first in the source file.
The superclass implementation.
A compile error is always reported.
questions.explanation: Class methods take priority over interface default methods.

questions.question: Can an interface extend multiple interfaces?
options: Yes.
No; interfaces can extend only one interface.
Yes, but only if they are in the same package.
No; only classes can extend multiple types.
questions.explanation: Interfaces support multiple inheritance of type.

questions.question: How does an abstract class differ from an interface?
options: An abstract class cannot have constructors; an interface can.
An abstract class cannot have methods; an interface can.
An abstract class can have instance state and constructors; an interface supports multiple inheritance of type and contracts.
They are identical; both can be extended by multiple classes.
questions.explanation: Interfaces can also provide default and static behavior.

questions.question: What is a functional interface?
options: An interface with no methods.
An interface with only default methods.
An interface with exactly one abstract method under the Java functional-interface rules.
An interface that can be instantiated using new.
questions.explanation: It can be implemented by a lambda or method reference.

questions.question: Is @FunctionalInterface required for lambda compatibility?
options: Yes; lambdas require the annotation.
No; it is only a compile-time check, not required for lambda use.
Yes, but only for generic interfaces.
Only inside the java.util.function package.
questions.explanation: The annotation asks the compiler to verify the interface's functional-interface status.

questions.question: What is a sealed class or interface?
options: A class that cannot have any subclasses.
A type that restricts which types may directly extend or implement it.
A class whose fields cannot be modified.
An interface that is hidden from other packages.
questions.explanation: Permitted direct subtypes declare an appropriate status such as final, sealed, or non-sealed.

questions.question: What does a Java record provide compared with a regular class?
options: A class whose fields can be modified through generated setters.
A class that supports multiple inheritance.
A concise data-oriented class with generated component accessors and equals, hashCode, and toString implementations.
A class that can be instantiated without constructors.
questions.explanation: Records are implicitly final and have final component fields, though referenced objects may be mutable.

questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
options: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; RuntimeException and Error subclasses are unchecked.
Checked exceptions are unchecked at runtime; unchecked are caught at compile time.
Unchecked exceptions must be declared; checked ones need not be.
Checked exceptions extend Error; unchecked ones extend Exception.
questions.explanation: Unchecked exceptions do not have the catch-or-declare requirement.

questions.question: What is the difference between throw and throws?
options: throw declares exceptions; throws raises an exception object.
They are interchangeable keywords.
throw throws an object; throws declares possible propagated exceptions.
throw is used in method signatures; throws is used in try blocks.
questions.explanation: One is an executable statement; the other is part of a method or constructor declaration.

questions.question: Does void test(){ throw new Exception(); } compile without a throws clause or catch?
options: No; a checked exception must be caught or declared.
Yes; Exception is unchecked.
Yes, but with a warning.
Yes, if the method is void.
questions.explanation: Exception is checked and must be caught or declared.

questions.question: Does void test(){ throw new RuntimeException(); } compile without a throws clause?
options: No; RuntimeException must be declared.
No; it must be caught.
Yes, but only with a warning.
Yes; RuntimeException is unchecked.
questions.explanation: RuntimeException is unchecked.

questions.question: What prints when a try block prints A, returns, and finally prints B?
options: B, then A
A, then B
A only
A, then B, then a runtime exception
questions.explanation: The finally block normally runs while control leaves the try statement.

questions.question: If try returns 1 and finally returns 2, what does the method return?
options: Compilation error
It throws an exception
questions.explanation: A return from finally overrides the pending return; this is discouraged.

questions.question: Does finally absolutely always execute?
options: Yes; it always runs in every possible situation.
Yes; even when the JVM exits via System.exit().
No; but only when an exception is thrown in try.
No; for example System.exit() or JVM termination can prevent it.
questions.explanation: Abrupt JVM or process termination, machine failure, or never reaching the exit path can prevent it.

questions.question: Can try appear without catch?
options: No; try must always have a catch.
Yes, but only with a throws clause.
No; try needs both catch and finally.
Yes; with finally or in a valid try-with-resources statement.
questions.explanation: A catch block is not mandatory in those forms.

questions.question: In what order should related exception types be caught?
options: More general types before more specific types.
Alphabetical order.
More specific types before more general types.
Order does not matter.
questions.explanation: A later catch for a subtype may be unreachable after a broader catch.

questions.question: What happens if a catch block throws another exception?
options: It is automatically swallowed.
The finally block is skipped.
The original exception replaces it.
The new exception propagates unless handled by an enclosing handler.
questions.explanation: The original can be retained as a cause or suppressed exception where appropriate.

questions.question: What is try-with-resources?
options: A construct that catches all exceptions.
A try block that executes multiple resource threads.
A construct that automatically closes AutoCloseable resources when leaving the statement.
A try block with automatic retry.
questions.explanation: Resources are closed even when the body throws.

questions.question: If a try-with-resources body and close() both throw, which is usually primary?
options: The close() exception; the body exception is suppressed.
Both are thrown at once.
The body exception; close exceptions are suppressed.
Neither; the exceptions are ignored.
questions.explanation: Suppressed exceptions preserve cleanup failures without replacing the primary failure.

questions.question: What does Throwable.getSuppressed() return?
options: The exceptions suppressed by that throwable.
The exceptions that caused this one.
The exceptions that were handled by a catch block.
The stack trace elements.
questions.explanation: Try-with-resources commonly uses suppression for exceptions thrown during closing.

questions.question: How do Exception and Error differ?
options: Error extends Exception; both are recoverable.
Exception extends Error; both are unchecked.
They are unrelated hierarchies.
Both extend Throwable; Error generally indicates serious problems applications are not ordinarily expected to recover from.
questions.explanation: Exception commonly represents conditions application code may handle.

questions.question: Can Java catch Throwable?
options: No; Throwable cannot be caught.
Yes, but catching it indiscriminately is usually poor practice.
Yes, and it is recommended as a default handler.
Only in the main method.
questions.explanation: It includes serious Error subclasses such as OutOfMemoryError.

questions.question: What is exception propagation?
options: An exception is rethrown automatically after the finally block.
An unhandled exception travels up the call stack until a matching handler is found or the thread terminates.
An exception travels to the next catch block in the same method.
An exception is automatically logged and ignored.
questions.explanation: Each caller can handle it or allow it to continue propagating.

questions.question: What contract connects equals() and hashCode()?
options: Equal hash codes imply equal objects.
Unequal objects must have unequal hash codes.
Objects with equal hash codes must always be equal.
Equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may share a hash code.
questions.explanation: Hash-based collections depend on this contract.

questions.question: What can go wrong if equals() is overridden but hashCode() is not?
options: Nothing; hashCode() is derived from equals() automatically.
A compile error is reported.
Objects can no longer be compared with ==.
Hash-based collections may fail to find equal objects or may behave unexpectedly.
questions.explanation: Equal objects can end up in different hash buckets if their hash codes differ.

questions.question: What properties should equals() satisfy?
options: Reflexivity only.
Symmetry and consistency, but not transitivity.
Reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, consistency, and false when compared with null.
They must always return true for non-null arguments.
questions.explanation: These properties make equality reliable across APIs and collections.

questions.question: For two new String("x") objects, what do equals() and hashCode()== comparison return?
options: true and false
false and true
false and false
true and true
questions.explanation: Equal strings compare equal and have equal hash codes.

questions.question: What is toString() used for?
options: Generating the object's hash code.
A string representation of an object.
Cloning the object.
Comparing objects for equality.
questions.explanation: Object's default representation is not a stable output contract.

questions.question: What does Object.getClass() return?
options: The declared type of the variable.
The superclass of the object.
The runtime class of the object.
The name of the package.
questions.explanation: getClass() is final and cannot be overridden.

questions.question: Is == appropriate for comparing enum constants?
options: Yes; each enum constant is a singleton, so == is safe and idiomatic.
No; equals() must be used.
Only inside switch statements.
Only for enums with no fields.
questions.explanation: Each enum constant is a unique instance, making identity comparison idiomatic.

questions.question: Why can mutating a HashMap key cause lookup problems?
options: If mutation changes equals() or hashCode(), lookup may search the wrong bucket.
The key's memory address changes.
HashMap always throws ConcurrentModificationException.
Mutation prevents the key from being garbage collected.
questions.explanation: Immutable keys are safer in hash-based collections.

questions.question: What do Java generics provide?
options: Runtime type checking and added casts.
Faster execution through specialization.
Support for multiple inheritance.
Compile-time type safety and fewer explicit casts.
questions.explanation: Parameterized types catch many type mismatches before runtime.

questions.question: Is List<String> a subtype of List<Object>?
options: Yes; because String is a subtype of Object.
No; Java generics are invariant.
Yes, but only when read-only.
Yes, via covariance.
questions.explanation: Allowing this assignment would let non-String objects enter a list intended for strings.

questions.question: Does List<Object> x = new ArrayList<String>(); compile?
options: No; it fails to compile because generics are invariant.
Yes; ArrayList<String> is a List<Object>.
Yes, with an unchecked warning.
Yes, but add() will fail.
questions.explanation: The generic type arguments are incompatible.

questions.question: What does ? extends Number permit when reading from a collection?
options: Values can be added as Number, but not read.
Values can be read and added freely.
Only null can be read.
Values can be read as Number, but adding a non-null Number is generally unsafe.
questions.explanation: The exact subtype is unknown, so an arbitrary Number might violate the collection's type.

questions.question: What does ? super Integer permit?
options: Only reading is allowed.
Only Number values can be added.
Neither adding nor reading is allowed.
Integer values can be added; retrieved elements are generally typed as Object.
questions.explanation: The actual collection element type may be Integer or a supertype.

questions.question: What does PECS mean?
options: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
Producer Super, Consumer Extends.
Produce Everything, Consume Safely.
Public Extends, Private Super.
questions.explanation: Use extends for sources of T and super for destinations that consume T, as a practical guideline.

questions.question: Why can't a generic class directly use new T()?
options: Because T may be an interface.
The concrete type argument is generally unavailable at runtime due to type erasure.
Because generics are only available at compile time for primitives.
Because new is disallowed in generic classes.
questions.explanation: A factory or suitable Class<T> token is a common alternative.

questions.question: Can you create new List<String>[10]?
options: Yes; it works like any other generic array.
No.
Yes, but only with a raw cast.
Only if the list is final.
questions.explanation: Generic array creation with a non-reifiable component type is prohibited.

questions.question: What is type erasure?
options: Generic types become interfaces at runtime.
The compiler duplicates classes per type argument.
Type arguments are stored in each object's header.
Most generic type parameters are removed from ordinary runtime representations after compile-time checking.
questions.explanation: The compiler inserts casts and bridge methods as needed; some generic metadata remains available through reflection.

questions.question: What is a raw type?
options: A generic type with a wildcard.
A generic class with only primitives.
A generic type used without type arguments, such as List.
A type that cannot be instantiated.
questions.explanation: Raw types support backward compatibility but weaken type checking.

questions.question: What is heap pollution?
options: A heap that has no free memory.
A heap full of unreachable objects.
A parameterized variable refers to an object not of the expected parameterized type.
A garbage collection pause.
questions.explanation: Raw types and unchecked operations can cause it.

questions.question: Can a generic class declare a static field of its class type parameter T?
options: No.
Yes; each instantiation has its own static field.
Yes, but only if T is bounded.
Yes, but only if the field is final.
questions.explanation: A static member belongs to the generic class, not a particular type parameterization.

questions.question: What is a bridge method?
options: A method that skips type checks.
A method that connects two classes in different packages.
A compiler-generated method that preserves polymorphism after type erasure or covariant return changes.
A method that is invoked only by reflection.
questions.explanation: It helps maintain correct overriding behavior after compilation.

questions.question: Compare ArrayList and LinkedList.
options: ArrayList is efficient for end insertion only; LinkedList for indexed access.
ArrayList offers efficient indexed access; LinkedList has linear indexed access and efficient end operations.
ArrayList is synchronized; LinkedList is not.
LinkedList is always faster than ArrayList for both access and insertion.
questions.explanation: LinkedList insertion/deletion is only efficient when the relevant node or position is already available.

questions.question: Compare HashSet and TreeSet.
options: HashSet sorts elements; TreeSet uses hashing.
TreeSet allows duplicates; HashSet does not.
HashSet is hash-based without sorted iteration; TreeSet keeps elements sorted.
They are identical aside from names.
questions.explanation: TreeSet basic operations are generally logarithmic time.

questions.question: Can HashSet retain duplicate elements according to equals()?
options: Yes; duplicates are allowed.
Yes, but only if the elements are strings.
No.
Only if hashCode() differs.
questions.explanation: Hash codes help locate candidates and equals() determines equality.

questions.question: Can HashMap contain null keys and values?
options: Yes; one null key and multiple null values are allowed.
No; HashMap does not allow null keys or values.
Only null values, not null keys.
Only multiple null keys.
questions.explanation: Other maps, such as ConcurrentHashMap, have different null restrictions.

questions.question: What happens when the same key is inserted into HashMap twice?
options: An exception is thrown.
The earlier value is kept.
Both values are stored as a list.
The later value replaces the earlier value for that key.
questions.explanation: A map stores at most one mapping per key according to its equality rules.

questions.question: Compare HashMap and TreeMap.
options: HashMap is hash-based without guaranteed sorted order; TreeMap sorts keys.
TreeMap is hash-based; HashMap sorts keys.
HashMap sorts keys; TreeMap guarantees insertion order.
Both sort keys in the same way.
questions.explanation: TreeMap uses natural ordering or a comparator.

questions.question: Compare Comparable and Comparator.
options: Comparable is an external ordering; Comparator is the natural ordering.
Comparable works only on strings.
They are interchangeable names for the same interface.
Comparable defines natural ordering via compareTo(); Comparator defines an external ordering via compare().
questions.explanation: Comparators allow multiple orderings for one type.

questions.question: How does ListIterator differ from Iterator?
options: ListIterator supports backward traversal, replacement, insertion, and index operations in addition to forward traversal.
ListIterator is forward-only.
ListIterator supports only removal.
ListIterator works on any Collection, including Set.
questions.explanation: Iterator provides forward traversal and optional removal.

questions.question: What is a fail-fast iterator?
options: An iterator that never throws exceptions.
An iterator that can iterate in reverse.
An iterator that locks the collection.
An iterator that may throw ConcurrentModificationException after certain external structural modifications.
questions.explanation: Fail-fast behavior is best-effort bug detection, not thread safety.

questions.question: Compare Collections.unmodifiableList() and List.of().
options: The former is an unmodifiable view of a backing list; List.of() returns an unmodifiable list and rejects null elements.
unmodifiableList() returns a deeply immutable copy; List.of() returns a view.
List.of() returns a modifiable list; unmodifiableList() does not.
They are identical in behavior and null handling.
questions.explanation: Neither makes mutable elements themselves immutable.

questions.question: Does an unmodifiable collection guarantee deeply immutable contents?
options: No.
Yes; contents are deeply immutable.
Yes, but only for primitive wrapper types.
Only if the collection is sorted.
questions.explanation: Elements may be mutable, and an unmodifiable view may reflect changes to its backing collection.

questions.question: What happens when add() is called on a list returned by List.of()?
options: The element is added.
NullPointerException
UnsupportedOperationException
IllegalArgumentException
questions.explanation: List.of() returns an unmodifiable list.

questions.question: What is the difference between Queue and Deque?
options: Queue commonly models processing order; Deque supports insertion and removal at both ends.
Queue is for sorted data; Deque is for unsorted data.
Deque is a queue that allows only removal at both ends.
They are identical interfaces.
questions.explanation: Deque can implement queue-like or stack-like behavior.

questions.question: Compare HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap.
options: HashMap is thread-safe and rejects nulls; ConcurrentHashMap allows them but is not thread-safe.
ConcurrentHashMap is designed for concurrent access and rejects null keys/values; HashMap is not safe for unsynchronized concurrent structural modification.
They are identical except for the package name.
ConcurrentHashMap keeps keys sorted; HashMap does not.
questions.explanation: Choose a concurrent map when concurrent access requirements call for it.

questions.question: What does computeIfAbsent() do?
options: It removes a key if its value is null.
It computes and associates a value when a key is absent or mapped to null, subject to the map contract.
It always replaces the existing value with a newly computed one.
It throws an exception when the key is absent.
questions.explanation: It returns the existing or computed value, or null if no non-null value is established.

questions.question: What is a lambda expression?
options: A class with a single method declared inside another class.
A named method that is stored in a variable.
A compile-time annotation for functional programming.
A concise implementation of a functional interface.
questions.explanation: For example, Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("Hello").

questions.question: What is a method reference?
options: A pointer to a memory address of a method.
A reflection call to a method by name at runtime.
A way to rename an existing method.
A compact reference to an existing method or constructor where a functional interface is expected.
questions.explanation: For example, names.forEach(System.out::println).

questions.question: Can a lambda reassign a captured local variable?
options: No; a captured local must be final or effectively final.
Yes; lambdas can reassign captured locals freely.
Yes, but only if the variable is volatile.
Only inside static methods.
questions.explanation: A lambda can read an effectively final local variable.

questions.question: Does int x=10; Runnable r=()->System.out.println(x); x++; compile?
options: No; x is not effectively final, so the lambda cannot capture it.
Yes; it prints 10.
Yes; it prints 11.
Yes, but throws an exception at runtime.
questions.explanation: Modifying x means it is not effectively final.

questions.question: Can a lambda mutate an array referenced by an effectively final local variable?
options: No; arrays are immutable when captured.
No; the array reference must be reassigned.
Yes; the reference is effectively final, so the array elements may change.
Only if the array is declared volatile.
questions.explanation: The reference cannot be reassigned, but the referenced array's contents can change.

questions.question: What is the difference between stream map() and filter()?
options: map retains elements matching a predicate; filter transforms them.
They are identical; only the names differ.
map works only on numbers; filter works only on strings.
map transforms elements; filter retains elements satisfying a predicate.
questions.explanation: They perform different intermediate pipeline operations.

questions.question: What is the difference between intermediate and terminal stream operations?
options: Intermediate operations build a generally lazy pipeline; terminal operations trigger processing.
Intermediate operations trigger processing; terminal operations build the pipeline.
Intermediate operations run eagerly; terminal operations run lazily.
Both run eagerly in the order declared.
questions.explanation: Examples of terminal operations include collect(), count(), and forEach().

questions.question: What does Stream.of(1,2,3).filter(n -> { System.out.print(n); return n > 1; }).findFirst() print?
questions.explanation: The pipeline evaluates elements as needed and stops after finding the first matching element, 2.

questions.question: Can a stream be reused after a terminal operation?
options: No; reuse may throw IllegalStateException.
Yes; a stream can be reused any number of times.
Yes, but only for sequential streams.
Yes, after calling reset().
questions.explanation: A stream is intended for one use.

questions.question: Compare findFirst() and findAny().
options: findFirst returns the last element; findAny returns the first.
findFirst requests the first element in encounter order; findAny permits any element.
findFirst works only on sorted streams; findAny on unsorted.
They are identical in every case.
questions.explanation: findAny can provide more flexibility for parallel processing.

questions.question: Compare Optional.orElse(value) and orElseGet(supplier).
options: orElse evaluates lazily; orElseGet evaluates eagerly.
They are identical in behavior.
orElse accepts a supplier; orElseGet accepts a value.
orElse evaluates its argument eagerly; orElseGet invokes its supplier only when empty.
questions.explanation: Use a supplier to defer potentially expensive default computation.

questions.question: If Optional.of("Java").orElse(getDefault()) is evaluated and getDefault() prints called, what prints?
options: called, then Java
Java, then called
Java only
called only
questions.explanation: The orElse argument is evaluated before the method call even though the optional has a value.

questions.question: Compare Stream.reduce() and collect().
options: reduce combines values into a result; collect performs a mutable reduction into a result container.
reduce is a mutable reduction; collect is an immutable reduction.
They are the same operation under different names.
reduce works only on parallel streams; collect on sequential streams.
questions.explanation: For example, collect can accumulate stream elements into a list.

questions.question: What is a parallel stream?
options: A stream that may process elements concurrently, commonly using the common fork/join pool.
A stream that always uses a dedicated thread per element.
A stream that processes elements on the GPU.
A stream that reads from multiple files simultaneously.
questions.explanation: Parallel execution is not always faster and shared mutable state can make it unsafe.

questions.question: Why should stream side effects be used carefully?
options: Laziness, permitted reordering, and parallel execution can cause unexpected results or races.
Side effects are always forbidden in streams.
Streams do not allow any lambda expressions.
Streams cannot call methods that have side effects.
questions.explanation: Prefer stateless transformations and explicit collection where appropriate.

questions.question: How do Arrays.stream(intArray) and Stream.of(intArray) differ for a primitive int array?
options: Both yield a Stream<int[]> for a primitive int array.
Arrays.stream(intArray) yields an IntStream; Stream.of(intArray) yields a Stream<int[]> when the array is passed as one argument.
Both yield an IntStream of its elements.
Arrays.stream yields a Stream<int[]>; Stream.of yields an IntStream.
questions.explanation: Primitive arrays need the primitive stream APIs for element-wise primitive processing.

questions.question: Conceptually, how do stack and heap memory differ?
options: The stack holds objects; the heap holds method frames.
Each thread has its own JVM stack for frames; objects and arrays are generally allocated on the heap.
Stack and heap are shared by all threads in the same way.
The heap is per thread; the stack is global.
questions.explanation: Actual physical placement can vary with JVM optimizations.

questions.question: When is an object eligible for garbage collection?
options: When it is set to null explicitly.
When it is no longer reachable through the runtime's relevant reachability mechanisms, subject to reference and finalization details.
When its method returns.
When System.gc() is called on it.
questions.explanation: Eligibility does not mean immediate collection.

questions.question: Can Java programs have memory leaks despite garbage collection?
options: No; garbage collection prevents all leaks.
Only in native code.
Only if finalize() is not overridden.
Yes; for example, objects kept reachable through forgotten references.
questions.explanation: Unintended retained references, such as unbounded caches or listeners, can keep objects reachable.

questions.question: Does System.gc() guarantee immediate garbage collection?
options: No; it is only a hint to the JVM.
Yes; the collection runs immediately.
Yes, but only for the young generation.
Yes, if the heap is full.
questions.explanation: It is only a request or suggestion to the JVM.

questions.question: Compare OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError.
options: OutOfMemoryError means stack overflow; StackOverflowError means heap exhaustion.
They are the same error under different names.
OutOfMemoryError indicates a required memory allocation cannot be satisfied; StackOverflowError commonly means a thread stack exceeded its limit.
Both occur only in recursive methods.
questions.explanation: Deep recursion is a common cause of StackOverflowError.

questions.question: If a method receives an int[] and changes a[0], can the caller observe it?
options: No; arrays are passed by deep copy.
No; changes are lost when the method returns.
Yes, because the copied reference still points to the same array.
Only if the array is declared final.
questions.explanation: Java passes the reference value by value; both references designate the same object.

questions.question: Can a Java method swap two caller variables by swapping its parameters?
options: No; parameters are copies of the caller's values.
Yes; Java passes primitives by reference.
Yes, but only for objects.
Yes, if the parameters are final.
questions.explanation: Reassigning local parameter variables does not reassign the caller's variables.

questions.question: Does two references failing == imply the referenced objects are collectible?
options: No.
Yes; the objects are definitely unreachable.
Yes; they will be collected immediately.
Yes, if the references are null.
questions.explanation: Identity comparison is unrelated to whether objects remain reachable.

questions.question: When does class initialization execute static initializers?
options: Every time an object is created.
As part of class initialization, coordinated once per defining class loader under normal JVM operation.
Once at JVM startup for all classes.
Every time a static method is called.
questions.explanation: Static initialization is not repeated for each instance.

questions.question: What are loading, linking, and initialization?
options: Loading runs static initializers; linking reads bytecode; initialization allocates memory.
Loading compiles source; linking verifies it; initialization executes main().
They are three names for the same step.
Loading obtains the class representation; linking includes verification, preparation, and resolution; initialization runs class initialization code.
questions.explanation: They are distinct phases of class lifecycle.

questions.question: Can two class loaders load classes with the same fully qualified name as different types?
options: No; the JVM forbids duplicate class names.
Yes; they are treated as distinct runtime types.
Only if they are in different packages.
Only for interface types.
questions.explanation: Class identity depends on binary name and defining class loader.

questions.question: What does the JIT compiler do?
options: It converts Java source code to bytecode.
It converts bytecode to Java source at runtime.
It compiles frequently executed bytecode into native machine code at runtime where beneficial.
It manages memory allocation for objects.
questions.explanation: The JVM can use interpretation and runtime compilation strategies.

questions.question: How does a process differ from a thread?
options: A process shares memory with other processes; threads have separate address spaces.
A process is a lightweight thread.
A process has its own operating-system-managed address space and resources; threads within it typically share process memory.
They are the same concept under different names.
questions.explanation: Threads maintain separate execution state while sharing much of the process's resources.

questions.question: What is the difference between Thread.start() and Thread.run()?
options: start() calls run() on the current thread; run() starts a new thread.
They are identical.
start() initiates a new thread; calling run() directly is an ordinary method call.
run() starts a daemon thread; start() starts a user thread.
questions.explanation: Direct run() does not create a new thread of execution.

questions.question: What does synchronized provide?
options: Atomic operations on primitives without locks.
Monitor-based mutual exclusion and memory-visibility guarantees.
Automatic thread creation.
Lock-free memory allocation.
questions.explanation: Synchronization actions on the same monitor establish happens-before relationships.

questions.question: Which monitor is locked by a synchronized instance method versus a static synchronized method?
options: The Class object for both.
The receiver object for both.
The thread object for instance methods; the Class object for static methods.
The receiver object for an instance method; the declaring class's Class object for a static method.
questions.explanation: They use different monitors.

questions.question: Can two threads simultaneously execute synchronized instance methods on the same object's monitor?
options: Yes; synchronized allows concurrent access.
Yes, if the threads are in the same ThreadGroup.
Only if one of the methods is static.
No; the monitor can be held by only one thread at a time (aside from reentrancy).
questions.explanation: Only one thread at a time can hold that monitor.

questions.question: What is a race condition?
options: A bug caused by too many threads being created.
A correctness problem dependent on timing or interleaving of insufficiently coordinated operations.
A compile-time error for conflicting variables.
A deadlock between two threads.
questions.explanation: Proper synchronization or atomic operations can prevent relevant races.

questions.question: Is count++ thread-safe on a shared plain int?
options: Yes; increment is atomic for int.
Yes, but only on 64-bit JVMs.
No; it is a read-modify-write sequence that can interleave.
Yes, if the variable is a local.
questions.explanation: It is a read-modify-write operation and concurrent updates can be lost.

questions.question: Does volatile make count++ atomic?
options: Yes; volatile makes all operations atomic.
Yes, but only for int.
No; volatile does not make a compound read-modify-write atomic.
Only on 64-bit JVMs.
questions.explanation: volatile provides visibility and ordering for the field, not atomicity for compound operations.

questions.question: Compare volatile and synchronized.
options: volatile provides mutual exclusion; synchronized provides only visibility.
They are identical.
volatile gives field visibility and ordering; synchronized also provides mutual exclusion and monitor-based visibility guarantees.
volatile can be used on methods; synchronized only on fields.
questions.explanation: Use synchronization or atomics for compound state updates.

questions.question: What is deadlock?
options: A thread that is waiting for I/O.
A thread that runs indefinitely.
A thread that has been interrupted.
Threads are permanently blocked waiting on resources held by one another in a dependency cycle.
questions.explanation: Consistent lock ordering can prevent common deadlock patterns.

questions.question: How do wait() and sleep() differ?
options: sleep() releases the monitor; wait() does not.
wait() releases the monitor it waits on; sleep() does not release monitors held by the sleeping thread.
Both release the monitor.
Neither releases the monitor.
questions.explanation: wait() must be called while holding the relevant object's monitor.

questions.question: Why call wait() inside a loop?
options: To make the thread sleep longer.
To make wait() non-interruptible.
To avoid InterruptedException.
Spurious wakeups are allowed and the condition may change before the monitor is reacquired.
questions.explanation: Recheck the condition after waking.

questions.question: Compare notify() and notifyAll().
options: notify wakes all waiting threads; notifyAll wakes one.
They are identical.
notify wakes one waiting thread; notifyAll wakes all threads waiting on that monitor.
notify wakes threads waiting on any monitor.
questions.explanation: Awakened threads still need to reacquire the monitor.

questions.question: What does Thread.join() do?
options: Starts another thread.
Waits for another thread to terminate.
Interrupts another thread.
Merges two threads into one.
questions.explanation: It coordinates completion between threads.

questions.question: What is a daemon thread?
options: A background thread that alone does not prevent JVM exit after all started non-daemon threads terminate.
A thread that runs only on a daemon process.
A thread with the highest priority.
A thread that cannot be interrupted.
questions.explanation: Daemon threads are not a substitute for orderly resource cleanup.

questions.question: Compare Runnable and Callable.
options: Runnable returns a result; Callable does not.
Both return a result.
Runnable has no result and cannot declare checked exceptions in run(); Callable returns a result and can throw checked exceptions.
Callable cannot throw checked exceptions; Runnable can.
questions.explanation: Callable is useful when tasks produce results.

questions.question: What is ExecutorService used for?
options: Compiling Java source in parallel.
Serializing objects to the disk.
Managing task execution and thread reuse separately from low-level thread creation.
Managing network sockets.
questions.explanation: It supports task submission, lifecycle management, and result handling.

questions.question: Compare Future and CompletableFuture.
options: Future is composable; CompletableFuture is only a blocking result.
Future represents an asynchronous result; CompletableFuture adds composable dependent stages and callback-style pipelines.
They are identical.
CompletableFuture is synchronous; Future is asynchronous.
questions.explanation: CompletableFuture supports more expressive asynchronous workflows.

questions.question: What does AtomicInteger provide?
options: Thread-local variables.
Synchronized collections.
Automatic memory management.
Atomic operations such as incrementAndGet() and compareAndSet().
questions.explanation: These operations avoid lost updates for the operations they make atomic.

questions.question: What is the Java Memory Model?
options: The rules for how the garbage collector works.
The rules governing visibility, ordering, and synchronization between threads.
The layout of the JVM heap.
The rules for class loading.
questions.explanation: Happens-before relationships are central to its guarantees.

questions.question: What is printed by System.out.println("A" == "A"); and System.out.println(new String("A") == "A");?
options: true, then true
true, then false
false, then true
false, then false
questions.explanation: The literals are interned; the new String is a distinct object.

questions.question: Does calling show(null) compile if overloads show(String) and show(Integer) both exist?
options: Yes; the String overload is chosen.
No; the call is ambiguous.
Yes; the Integer overload is chosen.
Yes; a NullPointerException is thrown at runtime.
questions.explanation: Neither String nor Integer is a subtype of the other, so neither overload is more specific.

questions.question: If overloads show(Object) and show(String) exist, which is chosen for show(null)?
options: show(Object)
show(String)
Compilation error (ambiguous)
A NullPointerException at runtime
questions.explanation: String is more specific than Object.

questions.question: Compare String.valueOf((Object)null) and ((String)null).toString().
options: Both return 'null'.
Both throw NullPointerException.
The first throws NullPointerException; the second returns 'null'.
The first returns "null"; the second throws NullPointerException.
questions.explanation: String.valueOf(Object) handles a null reference, whereas invoking a method on null fails. An uncast String.valueOf(null) call can be ambiguous.

questions.question: What is the result of int x = 10; System.out.println(x == 10.0);?
options: false
Compilation error
true
ClassCastException at runtime
questions.explanation: Numeric promotion permits comparison after converting the integer to a compatible floating-point type.

questions.question: How do break and continue differ?
options: break skips to the next iteration; continue exits the loop.
break exits the relevant loop or switch; continue advances to the next iteration of the relevant loop.
They are identical.
break exits the method; continue exits the loop.
questions.explanation: Labeled forms can target an enclosing statement or loop.

questions.question: What does a for loop with i=0; i<3; i++ print when it prints i each iteration?
questions.explanation: Initialization runs once, the condition is checked before each iteration, and the update follows each completed iteration.

questions.question: How do for and while loops differ conceptually?
options: for loops can only iterate over collections; while loops cannot.
while loops always execute at least once.
They are identical in every way.
for groups initialization, condition, and update; while emphasizes a condition-controlled loop.
questions.explanation: Neither form is inherently faster in all circumstances.

questions.question: How does do-while differ from while?
options: do-while checks before the body; while checks after.
They are identical.
do-while checks after the body and executes at least once; while checks first.
while executes at least once; do-while may execute zero times.
questions.explanation: The condition's position determines whether the body can be skipped.

questions.question: Since which Java version can switch use String values?
options: Java 5
Java 8
Java 11
Java 7
questions.explanation: String support in switch was introduced in Java 7.

questions.question: Compare == and equalsIgnoreCase() for strings.
options: == compares contents; equalsIgnoreCase() compares references.
Both are case-sensitive.
They are identical.
== compares reference identity; equalsIgnoreCase() compares contents without distinguishing case under its rules.
questions.explanation: Use a content comparison rather than identity when checking textual equality.

questions.question: Is Java pass-by-reference or pass-by-value?
options: Always pass-by-reference.
Always pass-by-value, including when the copied value is an object reference.
Pass-by-reference for objects; pass-by-value for primitives.
Pass-by-name for objects.
questions.explanation: Reassigning a parameter does not reassign the caller's variable.

questions.question: Can an interface be implemented using an anonymous class?
options: Yes; an anonymous class can implement an interface.
No; interfaces can only be implemented by named classes.
Only if the interface has default methods.
Only for functional interfaces.
questions.explanation: An anonymous class can provide required interface method implementations.

questions.question: Can a lambda replace every anonymous class?
options: Yes; lambdas can replace all anonymous classes.
Yes, but only inside static methods.
No; for instance, lambdas cannot implement interfaces with multiple abstract methods.
Yes, if the class has a single method.
questions.explanation: Lambdas require a functional interface and have different this semantics; anonymous classes can declare extra state and methods.

questions.question: What does var mean in Java?
options: Local variable type inference; the variable still has a static type inferred from its initializer.
Declares a variable whose type can change at runtime.
Declares a dynamically typed variable.
Declares an untyped variable like in JavaScript.
questions.explanation: Introduced in Java 10; var is not a dynamic type and is not allowed for fields or method parameters.

questions.question: How do var x = "Java" and Object y = "Java" differ in static type?
options: Both are Object.
x is Object; y is String.
x is String; y is Object.
Both are String.
